     1→# Project: Code Evolution — LLM-Designed Adapter Architectures for Time Series Foundation Models
     2→
     3→NeurIPS 2026 submission. LLM-guided evolutionary search generates PyTorch `nn.Module` adapter code for the MOMENT time series foundation model, searching an unbounded architecture space where LLM guidance genuinely outperforms discrete hyperparameter search.
     4→
     5→## Architecture
     6→
     7→```
     8→feasibility/          Core library (importable modules)
     9→scripts/              Modal GPU runners (entrypoints)
    10→results/              Experiment outputs (JSON logs, comparisons)
    11→template_code/        [LEGACY] Vendored TEMPLATE transferability code
    12→```
    13→
    14→GPU computation runs on **Modal.com** (A10G). LLM calls (OpenAI gpt-4o-mini) run locally. Data serialized as numpy for Modal containers.
    15→
    16→## Active Modules
    17→
    18→| Module | Purpose |
    19→|--------|---------|
    20→| `feasibility/code_evolution.py` | Core method — `CodeIndividual`, `validate_adapter_code()`, `train_adapter_from_code()`, `llm_generate_code()`, `run_code_evolution()` |
    21→| `feasibility/modal_app.py` | Modal app/image, remote GPU functions: `evaluate_config`, `finetune_config`, `compute_statistics_remote` |
    22→| `feasibility/model.py` | `load_moment()`, encoder block discovery, `_apply_unfreeze()`, LoRA/bottleneck attachment, hook registration |
    23→| `feasibility/finetune.py` | `finetune_forecasting()` / `finetune_classification()`, head factories (`LinearHead`, `MLPHead`), pooling |
    24→| `feasibility/data.py` | 7 forecasting loaders (ETTh1/h2/m1/m2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic), 2 classification, serialize/deserialize |
    25→| `feasibility/config.py` | `AdapterConfig` dataclass, discrete search space constants (2,160 configs) |
    26→| `scripts/run_code_evolution.py` | Main experiment script — CLI args: `--seed`, `--dataset`, `--n-generations`, `--pop-size`, `--model` |
    27→
    28→## Baseline Modules (kept for comparison, do not extend)
    29→
    30→| Module | Purpose |
    31→|--------|---------|
    32→| `feasibility/evolution.py` | Traditional evo search — `Individual`, crossover, mutation, tournament selection |
    33→| `feasibility/llm_operators.py` | LLM-guided discrete hyperparameter evolution (OpenAI function calling) |
    34→| `scripts/run_evolution.py` | Traditional evo runner |
    35→| `scripts/run_llm_evolution.py` | Discrete LLM evo runner |

    38→
    39→- `feasibility/scores.py`, `feasibility/features.py`, `template_code/` — TEMPLATE transferability (scores don't predict MSE)

    43→
    44→## Code Evolution Interface
    45→
    46→Adapter contract:
    47→```python
    48→class Adapter(nn.Module):
    49→    def __init__(self, d_model: int, output_dim: int):
    50→        super().__init__()
    51→        # d_model=768 (MOMENT hidden dim), output_dim=96 (forecast horizon)
    52→
    53→    def forward(self, hidden_states: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    54→        """(batch, seq_len=512, d_model=768) -> (batch, output_dim=96)"""
    55→```
    56→
    57→Constraints: max 500K params, only `torch`/`nn`/`F`/`math` imports. Backbone: MOMENT with last-4 encoder layers unfrozen.
    58→
    59→## Data Flow
    60→
    61→```
    62→LLM (gpt-4o-mini) → adapter code strings
    63→  → Local CPU validation (exec, shape check, param count ≤ 500K)
    64→  → Valid codes → Modal GPU starmap (3-epoch train) → MSE
    65→  → Invalid codes → fitness=-inf, error fed back to LLM
    66→  → Elitism (top-2) + 18 LLM offspring → next generation
    67→  → After 12 gens: top-5 validated at 15 epochs
    68→```

```
     1→# Research Status: Raw-Routed Adapters and Architecture Search for TSFMs
     2→
     3→**Target:** NeurIPS 2026 (Abstract: May 4, Paper: May 6)
     4→**Last updated:** 2026-04-04
     5→**Estimated acceptance:** 85-90% (Strong Accept / Spotlight tier)
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## The Paper in One Sentence
    10→
    11→We discovered that TSFM backbone normalization destroys MoE routing signals (1/18 wins), and propose Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA) that routes on the raw input instead (17/18 wins, -56% MSE), using diverse expert adapters discovered by Adapter Architecture Search (AAS).
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## Three Contributions (The "Triple Threat")
    16→
    17→### 1. The Diagnostic Insight: Time-Series Discretization Gap
    18→- TSFM LayerNorm homogenizes hidden states → standard MoE routing collapses
    19→- AdaMix (hidden-state routing): **1/18 wins** (routing entropy → 0)
    20→- DARTS supernet: **1/6 wins** after discretization
    21→- This is specific to frozen-backbone TSFMs (not generic NAS failure)
    22→
    23→### 2. The Method: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)
    24→- Routes on raw unnormalized input, experts process backbone embeddings
    25→- **17/18 wins, average -56% MSE improvement**
    26→- Routing entropy 1.4-1.6 / 1.61 max (genuinely diverse, non-collapsed)
    27→- Same experts as AdaMix — only the routing signal source changes
    28→
    29→### 3. The Search Space: Adapter Architecture Search (AAS)
    30→- Formal hierarchy: C ⊂ G_tmpl ⊂ G_code with strict subsumption proof
    31→- 25/25 wins with random template search (search space > algorithm)
    32→- Discovers cross-domain patterns: depthwise conv, BatchNorm, feature attention
    33→- 63% of discovered adapters Pareto-dominate baselines (lower MSE AND fewer params)
    34→- Budget sufficiency: f ≈ 0.03-0.05, B ≥ 60 suffices for 95% success
    35→
    36→### Bonus: T-ZCP (Zero-Cost Proxy)
    37→- Gradient norm at initialization predicts trained MSE
    38→- ρ = 0.905 on Electricity, ρ > 0.7 on 3/6 datasets
    39→- Reduces search cost from 30 min to 300ms (on compatible datasets)
```

```
    51→\begin{abstract}
    52→Adapting pretrained time series foundation models (TSFMs) to downstream tasks currently relies on static, single-head adapters. While dynamically routing across diverse adapter topologies via mixture-of-experts (MoE) offers a path to task-specific specialization, we identify a fatal structural bottleneck in temporal adaptation: \textbf{gradient co-adaptation}. We demonstrate that standard MoE routing on TSFM hidden states collapses to a single expert---routing entropy dropping to $0.000\pm0.000$ (3 seeds)---on backbones with internal Reversible Instance Normalization (RevIN), particularly when backbone layers are unfrozen. A cross-backbone control on Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} (which lacks RevIN) confirms that the collapse is \emph{normalization-induced}, not inherent to MoE routing on temporal representations.
    53→To break this collapse, we propose \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}. RR-MoA routes on the raw, \emph{pre-normalization} input signal via a lightweight gating network, preserving the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips. A direct ablation confirms that applying per-window RevIN to the router's input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$, empirically isolating rawness as the source of the gains. Crucially, we uncover a \textbf{``Frozen Paradox''}: keeping the backbone strictly frozen yields \emph{superior} MoE routing compared to standard partial fine-tuning. Evaluated across three architecturally distinct backbones (MOMENT-small, MOMENT-large, Moirai), strictly frozen RR-MoA achieves \textbf{54/54 wins} against single-adapter baselines ($p{<}0.02$, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and significantly outperforms LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, TRACE-style multi-scale adapters~\citep{li2025trace}, and independent expert ensembles under identical protocols. On Moirai+RR-MoA, the frozen-backbone paradigm reaches $0.209$ MSE on Weather---matching DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} trained from scratch ($0.208$). We provide an information-theoretic argument explaining why RevIN destroys routing and validate it empirically: expert selection correlates with precisely the temporal statistics (amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips. Top-2 sparse routing bounds active expert FLOPs to $40\%$ of a dense mixture while preserving the MSE gains.
    54→\end{abstract}
    55→
    56→\section{Introduction}
    57→\label{sec:intro}
    58→
    59→The transformer architecture~\citep{vaswani2017attention} has enabled foundation models~\citep{bommasani2021foundation} across language~\citep{devlin2019bert, brown2020gpt3} and vision~\citep{dosovitskiy2021vit}. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer/Timer-XL~\citep{liu2024timer, liu2025timerxl}, Moirai/Moirai-MoE~\citep{woo2024moirai, liu2025moiraimoe}, UniTS~\citep{lee2024units}, Lag-Llama~\citep{rasul2024lagllama}, Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, and TTM~\citep{ekambaram2024ttm} have emerged as powerful pretrained representations for temporal tasks. Once a TSFM is pretrained, a concrete practical question determines whether it is useful in production: \textit{how should the adapter that connects it to a downstream task be designed and trained?}
    60→
    61→\textbf{The one-size-fits-all adapter status quo.} Current TSFM adaptation almost always reduces to the same computational template: \emph{pool the backbone's hidden states $\to$ project to the output horizon}, with a handful of standard variants---linear probing~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm}, MLP heads~\citep{nie2023patchtst, wu2023timesnet}, LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, and bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}. Crucially, every public TSFM benchmark we are aware of uses a \emph{single static} adapter for an entire dataset. Yet real time series are highly non-stationary: a dataset such as ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions, and it is far from obvious that a single adapter topology is optimal for every window. This observation motivates a \emph{mixture of adapters}: maintain a small pool of topologically distinct expert heads and let a learned router assign each window to the most appropriate expert per sample.
    62→
    63→\textbf{Why frozen at all?} Lightweight supervised baselines (DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear}) achieve materially lower absolute MSE than any frozen-backbone adapter on the same evaluation scale. Our contribution is not to replace single-dataset specialists but to optimize routing within the frozen-backbone paradigm motivated by (i)~multi-tenant cloud serving with hot-swappable per-tenant adapters, (ii)~on-device deployment where per-site retraining is infeasible, and (iii)~cross-task reuse where one backbone drives forecasting and imputation via different expert pools (Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes the only viable per-dataset adaptation path.
    64→
    65→\textbf{The natural idea that fails: MoE on TSFMs.} When we apply the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---to a TSFM with internal RevIN, it \emph{collapses catastrophically}. Across 3 seeds, 3 datasets, and every setting where backbone layers are unfrozen, routing entropy drops to exactly $0.000\pm0.000$ (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}): all weight concentrates on a single expert.
    66→
    67→\textbf{Diagnosis: normalization-induced co-adaptation.} The collapse has a specific causal structure: whichever expert the router marginally prefers receives larger gradients; those flow back into the unfrozen backbone, which reshapes $\mathbf{H}$ to serve that expert better, completing a positive feedback loop within ${\sim}50$ steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Freezing $\theta$ breaks this loop (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}: entropy recovers to $0.5$--$0.6$), but hidden-state routing still underperforms because the backbone's internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that would distinguish samples. A controlled ablation (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}) confirms this: applying RevIN to the router's input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$. A cross-backbone control on Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} (which lacks RevIN) shows that AdaMix routing \emph{does not collapse} even with unfrozen layers (entropy $1.48$--$1.60$; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}), confirming that the failure is normalization-specific, not inherent to MoE on temporal data.
    68→
    69→\textbf{Our fix.} We propose \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}: (i)~the router reads the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ (preserving per-window trend, amplitude, volatility), and (ii)~the backbone is kept strictly frozen ($\texttt{requires\_grad}{=}\texttt{False}$ for all $\theta$). Only the router and experts are trainable, reducing the optimization from $\theta_\text{active}\cup\phi\cup\psi$ to $\phi\cup\psi$ alone.
    70→
    71→\textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} In our 3\,datasets\,$\times$\,3\,freeze levels\,$\times$\,3\,seeds ablation (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), strictly frozen RR-MoA is at least as good as partially unfrozen RR-MoA on every dataset, with $43.5\%$ and $51.1\%$ MSE reductions on ETTh1 and ETTm1. Unfreezing buys routing collapse, not expressivity---reversing the standard NLP PEFT heuristic.
    72→
    73→\textbf{Populating the expert pool.} For RR-MoA to work, the expert pool must be diverse. We formalize \textbf{Adapter Architecture Search (AAS)} as an LLM-guided code-level search over arbitrary PyTorch \texttt{nn.Module} programs that \emph{recovers} cross-domain motifs---depthwise convolutions~\citep{howard2017mobilenets}, BatchNorm~\citep{he2016resnet, ioffe2015batchnorm}, feature attention~\citep{hu2018senet}---into the TSFM adapter vocabulary. We distill the search logs into five canonical expert topologies used in all RR-MoA experiments.
    74→
    75→Our contributions: \textbf{(1)}~We diagnose \emph{normalization-induced co-adaptation} as the cause of MoE routing collapse on TSFMs with RevIN: entropy $0.000\pm0.000$ whenever backbone layers are unfrozen, confirmed absent on RevIN-free Moirai (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). \textbf{(2)}~We propose \textbf{RR-MoA}, which routes on the raw pre-normalization signal and keeps the backbone frozen, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} across 6 datasets, 3 freeze levels, and 3 seeds against single-adapter baselines, and significantly outperforming LoRA, TRACE-style adapters, and independent ensembles ($p{<}0.02$, Wilcoxon; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). \textbf{(3)}~RR-MoA generalizes across three architecturally distinct backbones (MOMENT-small/large, Moirai), with Moirai+RR-MoA matching DLinear on Weather (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). \textbf{(4)}~We uncover the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: strictly frozen routing outperforms partially unfrozen routing, reversing the standard PEFT heuristic. \textbf{(5)}~We provide an information-theoretic argument explaining why RevIN collapses routing and validate it via per-sample routing analysis (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). \textbf{(6)}~Top-2 sparse routing bounds active FLOPs to $40\%$ of a dense mixture (\S\ref{sec:topk}).
    76→
    77→\textbf{Gaps.} Recent NeurIPS 2025 work searches over finetuning \textit{strategies} (MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft}), \textit{pruning} (Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune}), or \textit{model selection} (TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template})---but none searches the adapter \textit{architecture}. In the LLM-guided search community, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo} and AI Research Agents~\citep{toledo2025aiagents} demonstrate code-level search for automated ML, but not for FM adaptation. We bridge these lines of work.
    78→
    79→\section{Related Work}
    80→
    81→\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} Standard adaptation uses LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} or bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters} with manually chosen configurations. MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning for encoder-based TSFMs. TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads---the closest work, but heads are hand-designed. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos. AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations. Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning. In-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} addresses model selection; GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} provides benchmarking. All search over finetuning \textit{strategies}, not adapter \textit{architecture}---the gap we address.
    82→
    83→\textbf{NAS for Adapters.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs. NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} integrates NAS for vision adapters. ONE-NAS~\citep{li2022onenas} and TS-NAS~\citep{liang2024tsnas} search raw time series architectures but not adapters on pretrained backbones. No prior work searches an \textit{unbounded} architecture space for TSFM adapters.
    84→
    85→\textbf{LLM-Guided Code Search.} LLMs trained on code~\citep{chen2021codex} enable program-level search. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, ELM~\citep{lehman2023elm}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo}, LLMatic~\citep{nasir2024llmatic}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, SOAR~\citep{pourcel2025soar}, EvoTune~\citep{surina2025evotune}, GENESYS~\citep{cheng2025genesys}, SEA-TS~\citep{xu2026seats}, and AI Research Agents~\citep{toledo2025aiagents} demonstrate evolutionary program synthesis across domains~\citep{sobania2023program, zhang2025llm4opt}. We apply this paradigm to TSFM adapter search---$1000\times$ cheaper than full-model evolution.
    86→
    87→\section{Method}
    88→\label{sec:method}

   160→
   161→\subsection{Problem Formulation}
   162→
   163→An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. An \emph{architecture space} $\mathcal{G}$ is a set of adapter specifications, each defining a computational graph, parameter space, and initialization (formal definitions in Appendix~\ref{app:formal_defs}).
   164→
   165→\begin{definition}[Adapter Architecture Search]
   166→\label{def:aas}
   167→Given backbone $f_\theta$, architecture space $\mathcal{G}$, and dataset $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_\text{train} \cup \mathcal{D}_\text{val} \cup \mathcal{D}_\text{test}$, the \textbf{AAS problem} is the bilevel optimization:
   168→\begin{equation}
   169→g^* = \arg\min_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \; \mathcal{L}\!\left(g_{\hat{\phi}} \circ f_{\hat{\theta}_\text{act}}, \; \mathcal{D}_\text{val}\right), \quad \text{where} \quad \{\hat{\phi}, \hat{\theta}_\text{act}\} = \arg\min_{\phi, \theta_\text{act}} \; \mathcal{L}\!\left(g_\phi \circ f_{\theta}, \; \mathcal{D}_\text{train}\right)
   170→\label{eq:aas}
   171→\end{equation}
   172→\end{definition}
   173→
   174→This separates two decisions conflated in current TSFM practice: \textit{what computational graph} the adapter should implement (outer loop) and \textit{what weights} that graph should have (inner loop).
   175→
   176→\subsection{Expert Pool Construction via Architecture Search}
   177→\label{sec:search_space}
   178→
   179→For RR-MoA to benefit from routing, the expert pool must contain topologically diverse adapters. We populate it via \textbf{Adapter Architecture Search (AAS)}: an LLM-guided code-level evolutionary search over arbitrary PyTorch \texttt{nn.Module} programs ($\leq 500$K params). AAS operates in an unbounded code space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ strictly containing the discrete hyperparameter space $\mathcal{C}$ and a template grammar space $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ (hierarchy proof and search details in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:grammar}, \ref{app:aas_details}). A population of 20 adapters evolves over 12 generations (${\sim}240$ evaluations, 3-epoch fitness probes on A10G). AAS recovers cross-domain motifs---depthwise convolutions~\citep{howard2017mobilenets}, Conv1d+BatchNorm~\citep{he2016resnet, ioffe2015batchnorm}, feature attention~\citep{hu2018senet}---absent from any published TSFM adapter.
   180→
   181→For all RR-MoA experiments, we use a fixed pool of five lightweight canonical expert heads (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool) rather than the AAS-discovered architectures. These canonical experts outperform the heavier AAS macro pool ($0.690$ vs $0.764$ on ETTh1) for routing, likely because lightweight experts produce sharper routing gradients. AAS's primary role is demonstrating that the \emph{code-level} search space contains strictly better single-adapter architectures ($-9\%$ MSE on average; Appendix~\ref{app:aas_results}); the routing framework is the core contribution.
   182→
   183→\textbf{Standard protocol.} Chronological train/val/test splits per the LTSF benchmark~\citep{zhou2021informer}: ETT-hourly (8640/2880/2880), ETT-minutely (34560/11520/11520), Weather/Electricity (60/20/20\%). Architecture search uses the validation set; final evaluation uses the test set.
   184→
   185→\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
   186→\label{sec:rrmoa}
   187→
   188→AAS discovers topologically diverse adapters, but deploying them individually requires per-dataset search. A natural alternative is MoE routing, but standard hidden-state routing \emph{collapses catastrophically} on TSFMs due to gradient co-adaptation (\S\ref{sec:intro}). We propose \textbf{RR-MoA}, which splits the information stream: the TSFM processes $\mathbf{H}$, while a lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to compute sparse Top-$k$ routing weights:
   189→\begin{equation}
   190→\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} \underbrace{\widetilde{w}_j}_{\text{sparse weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM})}_{\text{deep embedding branch}},\quad
   191→\mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}),\, k\right),\;\;
   192→\widetilde{w} = \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})\right)
   193→\label{eq:rrmoa}
   194→\end{equation}
   195→where $G_\psi$ is a small Conv1d\,+\,pooling\,+\,linear gate ($\sim$1.1K params) operating directly on the raw time series, and each $\text{Expert}_k$ is an AAS-distilled adapter head. Routing is restricted to the Top-$k$ experts with the highest gate logits, so only $k$ of $K$ experts execute per sample. With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.
   196→

   198→\caption{RR-MoA: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters with Top-$k$ sparse routing}
   199→\label{alg:rrmoa}
   200→\begin{algorithmic}[1]
```

```
   200→\begin{algorithmic}[1]
   201→\REQUIRE Strictly frozen TSFM $f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}$, raw input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L}$, $K$ expert adapters, sparsity $k\leq K$
   202→\STATE $\mathbf{H}\leftarrow f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Deep embeddings; \textbf{no gradients} through $\theta$}
   203→\STATE $\mathbf{g}\leftarrow G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Raw-signal gate logits, $\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times K}$}
   204→\STATE $\mathcal{T}\leftarrow \mathrm{TopK}(\mathbf{g},\,k)$ \hfill \COMMENT{Per-sample indices of the $k$ selected experts}
   205→\STATE $\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}\leftarrow \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathbf{g})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Renormalized over selected experts only}
   206→\STATE \textbf{for each}\ $j \in \mathcal{T}$\ \textbf{do}
   207→\STATE \quad $\mathbf{o}_j\leftarrow \text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Only the $k$ selected experts execute}
   208→\STATE \textbf{end for}
   209→\STATE $\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow \sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{w}_j\cdot \mathbf{o}_j$
   210→\RETURN $\mathbf{Y}$
   211→\end{algorithmic}
   212→\end{algorithm}

   214→\section{Experiments}
   215→
   216→\subsection{Setup}
   217→
   218→\textbf{Backbones.} Our primary backbone is MOMENT-small~\citep{goswami2024moment} ($d_\text{model}{=}512$, 8 T5-style encoder blocks, internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}). We additionally evaluate MOMENT-large ($d_\text{model}{=}1024$, 24 blocks) and Moirai-1.1-R-small~\citep{woo2024moirai} ($d_\text{model}{=}384$, 6 blocks, no RevIN), testing cross-backbone generalization in \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}. Primary results use a \emph{strictly frozen} backbone ($\theta$ not updated); freeze-level ablations appear in \S\ref{sec:freeze_ablation}.
   219→
   220→\textbf{MSE scale.} All MSE values are reported on channel-wise StandardScaler-normalized inputs, the standard LTSF convention~\citep{zhou2021informer, nie2023patchtst}. As a calibration anchor, DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} on our pipeline achieves $0.416$ (ETTh1), $0.322$ (ETTm1), $0.208$ (Weather)---consistent with published numbers (Appendix~\ref{app:dlinear}).
   221→
   222→\textbf{Datasets and tasks.} ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather (21 channels), and Electricity (321 channels)---standard LTSF benchmarks~\citep{godahewa2021monash, wen2023tssurvey}. Chronological train/val/test splits follow the LTSF protocol. We evaluate both long-term forecasting ($H{=}96$) and masked imputation (20\% reconstruction).
   223→
   224→\textbf{Training.} Adam optimizer, lr$=10^{-3}$, MSE loss, batch size 128, 15 epochs. Adapter architecture search (during AAS) uses 3-epoch fitness probes on the validation split; final reported numbers are 15-epoch test MSE. Multi-seed experiments use seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.
   225→
   226→\textbf{Baselines.} We compare against six baselines under the identical strictly frozen protocol: (i)~three hand-designed \textit{fixed adapters} (linear, attention, conv---representing standard TSFM practice), (ii)~\textit{LoRA}~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep over rank, targets, and heads; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), (iii)~a \textit{TRACE-style} multi-scale adapter~\citep{li2025trace} (multi-scale convolutions + gated importance weighting; no public code available, we implement the core ideas), (iv)~an \textit{independent ensemble} of the same 5 expert heads trained separately and averaged at inference (isolating routing from expert diversity), (v)~\textit{AdaMix}~\citep{wang2022adamix} (standard hidden-state MoE routing), and (vi)~\textit{DLinear}~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} as a supervised calibration anchor (not a competitor). All frozen-backbone baselines use identical training setup.
   227→
   228→\textbf{Reproducibility.} All code, raw JSON results, per-seed routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data are included in the supplementary material and will be open-sourced upon acceptance.
   229→
   230→\subsection{Main Results: AAS and Cross-Backbone}
   231→\label{sec:main_results}
   232→
   233→AAS wins all 20 single-adapter experiments on MOMENT-small across 6 datasets and horizons H=96--720 (average $-9.0\%$ MSE vs.\ best fixed adapter; full grid in Appendix~\ref{app:aas_results}, Table~\ref{tab:main}). AAS also generalizes across backbones: it wins on MOMENT-large ($d_\text{model}{=}1024$, 24 blocks) and Moirai-1.1-R-small, with improvements of $-3.0\%$ to $-18.0\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_results}, Table~\ref{tab:backbone}). AAS is used here primarily to populate the RR-MoA expert pool; the core contribution is the routing framework below.
   234→
   235→\subsection{Search Space Decomposition and Expert Pool}
   236→\label{sec:architectures}
   237→
   238→A factorial decomposition (Appendix~\ref{app:decomposition}) confirms that the code space is the dominant factor: LLM-discovered adapters achieve $19.6\%$ lower MSE than template-space adapters ($p{=}0.003$, Cohen's $d{=}0.67$). AAS recovers cross-domain motifs---depthwise convolutions~\citep{howard2017mobilenets}, Conv1d+BatchNorm~\citep{he2016resnet, ioffe2015batchnorm}, feature attention~\citep{hu2018senet}---absent from any published TSFM adapter (Appendix~\ref{app:architectures}). To isolate routing efficacy from expert capacity, we distill the AAS logs into five lightweight archetypes (mean, last-token, max, attention, Conv1d pooling) used as the fixed expert pool in all RR-MoA experiments. We also evaluate a ``macro'' pool of five AAS-discovered architectures (Conv1d+BatchNorm+residual, depthwise separable, multi-scale conv, gated conv, BN+mean; $271$K total params) in the Frozen Paradox ablation (\S\ref{sec:freeze_ablation}). The canonical pool outperforms the macro pool on MOMENT-small ($0.690$ vs $0.764$ on ETTh1), likely because lightweight experts produce sharper routing gradients; the macro pool's value is in stress-testing the Frozen Paradox at higher adapter capacity.
   239→
   240→\subsection{RR-MoA: Routing Collapse and Its Resolution}
   241→\label{sec:freeze_ablation}
   242→
   243→Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa} presents the central experimental result of the paper. Using the \emph{same five expert adapter heads} (mean, last-token, max, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool) in all three rows, we compare Top-2 RR-MoA against the single best fixed adapter baseline across a full grid of 3 datasets $\times$ 3 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds. RR-MoA wins \textbf{27 out of 27} configurations with tight standard deviations.

RR-MoA wins \textbf{54/54} configurations across 6 datasets (extended grid: ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}); the improvement is largest under the strictly frozen backbone (``Frozen Paradox'').}

   271→
   272→\textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} On ETTh1 and ETTm1, the \emph{strictly frozen} backbone yields RR-MoA's best absolute MSE; on Weather, last-2 is marginally better ($-47.2\%$ vs $-44.6\%$). Across all 6 datasets (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}), strictly frozen is the best configuration on 4 and within $13\%$ on the remaining 2, \emph{reversing} the standard NLP PEFT heuristic. The mechanism is Table~\ref{tab:adamix}: unfreezing the backbone is precisely what destroys routing diversity. We verify this paradox is not an artifact of low adapter capacity: repeating the ablation with the AAS-discovered macro expert pool ($271$K params, $9\times$ the canonical pool) shows frozen is still best on ETTh1 ($0.764{\pm}0.015$ vs $0.806{\pm}0.128$ for last-4), while ETTm1 and Weather show partial recovery under unfreezing ($0.510$ vs $0.583$ on ETTm1). The boundary is adapter capacity: low-capacity experts cannot exploit the additional gradient signal from unfreezing, while high-capacity experts can partially recover---but frozen routing remains competitive in all cases.
   273→
   274→\textbf{Routing vs.\ ensembling.} Replacing the learned router with a fixed uniform mixture ($w_k = 1/K$) degrades performance by $30$--$75\%$ on every dataset (ETTh1: $0.899$ vs $0.690$; ETTm1: $1.002$ vs $0.572$; Weather: $0.494$ vs $0.289$). Training the same 5 experts \emph{independently} and averaging predictions (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, ``Ind.\ Ensemble'') is $36$--$46\%$ worse than RR-MoA, confirming that learned per-sample routing---not merely expert diversity---is the source of the gains.

Under the strictly frozen setting entropy recovers ($0.3$--$1.0$), but MSE is still dominated by RR-MoA. Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} provides per-step mechanistic evidence: under unfreezing (red), entropy collapses within ${\sim}50$ gradient steps as the dominant expert's gradient norm grows and others starve; under freezing (blue), entropy remains stable near $1.5$.

(b)~Per-expert gradient L2 norm (unfrozen only): the dominant expert's gradient grows while the others starve, confirming the gradient co-adaptation feedback loop of \S\ref{sec:rrmoa}.    338→RR-MoA significantly outperforms every frozen-backbone baseline ($p{<}0.001$ for 4 of 5 baselines, $p{<}0.01$ for LoRA; Wilcoxon signed-rank, Bonferroni-corrected for 5 comparisons across 6 datasets$\times$3 seeds; Cohen's $d{=}1.0$--$4.1$). The independent ensemble---same experts, no router---is $36$--$46\%$ worse, confirming that learned per-sample routing adds substantial value beyond expert diversity alone. The TRACE-style multi-scale adapter and best LoRA from a 108-run sweep both fail to close the gap: neither multi-scale convolutions nor low-rank backbone perturbations substitute for raw-signal routing over diverse topologies.

On MOMENT-small, this gap is $40$--$60\%$; however, on Moirai the gap narrows dramatically (Weather: $0.209$ vs $0.208$; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
   341→
   342→\textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass.} To isolate whether RR-MoA's advantage comes from bypassing the backbone or specifically from reading the raw pre-normalization signal, we replace the router's input with the same signal after per-window RevIN (zero mean, unit variance). Everything else is identical.

The final column reports relative MSE \emph{degradation} of the RevIN router against the raw router --- \textbf{positive values mean the raw router is better}. Stripping the rawness degrades MSE by 60--88\% across all three datasets, confirming that routing on the backbone's post-normalization representation is insufficient: the per-window trend/amplitude/volatility that the normalization cascade removes are precisely the statistics the router relies on.}

   359→
   360→The RevIN router suffers $60$--$88\%$ MSE degradation on every dataset: bypass alone is insufficient; the \emph{content} of the raw signal matters. Routing entropy remains high ($1.50$--$1.57$), but the gate can no longer make discriminative decisions without per-window temporal statistics.
   361→
   362→\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: an information-theoretic argument.} The router's discriminative power depends on the variance of its gate logits across input windows: $\text{Var}_i[\mathbf{g}_i]$ where $\mathbf{g}_i = G_\psi(\mathbf{x}_i) \in \mathbb{R}^K$. When logit variance is low, the softmax outputs approach uniform and the router cannot specialize. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ can be decomposed into three components: mean level $\mu_i$ (trend), scale $\sigma_i$ (amplitude), and shape $\mathbf{s}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_i)/\sigma_i$ (normalized waveform). RevIN sets $\mu_i{=}0$, $\sigma_i{=}1$ for all $i$, so $\text{Var}_i[\mathbf{g}_i] \propto \text{Var}_i[\mathbf{s}_i]$ only---the two most discriminative statistics (mean and scale) are collapsed to constants. Without RevIN, $\text{Var}_i[\mathbf{g}_i] \propto \text{Var}_i[\mu_i, \sigma_i, \mathbf{s}_i]$---strictly richer. This explains all empirical observations: (i)~RevIN router loses $60$--$88\%$ MSE because the gate sees less variance; (ii)~Moirai (no RevIN) retains routing diversity even with unfrozen layers because the gate has full access to $(\mu, \sigma, \mathbf{s})$; (iii)~Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz} confirms that expert selection correlates with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips. When backbone layers are unfrozen, the co-adaptation loop (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}) amplifies the RevIN-induced signal poverty: the low-variance routing gradient gets dominated by whichever expert the backbone marginally reinforces, collapsing to a single expert within ${\sim}50$ steps.
   363→
   364→\textbf{What the router learns.} Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz} visualizes per-sample expert selection against temporal statistics. On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$ of windows), while Expert~2 (max-pool) preferentially handles low-amplitude, low-volatility windows (amp${\approx}1.2$, vol${\approx}0.06$) and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude, high-volatility windows (amp${\approx}5.1$, vol${\approx}0.50$). The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the tails of the distribution. On Weather, the distribution shifts: Expert~2 dominates ($69\%$), consistent with Weather's lower overall volatility. Expert selection correlates with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN would strip---confirming the information-theoretic argument above.
```

```
   408→\subsection{Cross-Backbone Generalization}
   409→\label{sec:cross_backbone}
   410→
   411→To verify that RR-MoA is not a MOMENT-specific trick, we evaluate on three architecturally distinct backbones: MOMENT-small (T5 encoder, 8 blocks, $d{=}512$, with RevIN), MOMENT-large (T5, 24 blocks, $d{=}1024$, with RevIN), and Moirai-1.1-R-small~\citep{woo2024moirai} (6 blocks, $d{=}384$, \textit{no RevIN}). All use strictly frozen backbones and Top-2 routing.
   412→
   413→\begin{table}[h]
   414→\centering

Best fixed column: strongest single-adapter baseline on that backbone (conv, seed 42). RR-MoA wins on all 9 backbone$\times$dataset configurations. Moirai achieves the best absolute MSE, matching DLinear on Weather ($0.209$ vs $0.208$).}

   432→
   433→Moirai+RR-MoA achieves the strongest absolute MSE across all three datasets, with Weather reaching $0.209{\pm}0.004$---effectively matching DLinear trained from scratch ($0.208{\pm}0.003$). This demonstrates that the frozen-backbone paradigm \emph{can} approach supervised performance when paired with an effective routing strategy and a sufficiently well-pretrained backbone.
   434→
   435→\textbf{Routing collapse is RevIN-specific.} Running AdaMix (hidden-state routing) on Moirai with last-4 unfreezing yields routing entropy $1.48$--$1.60$ (near the maximum of $\log 5 \approx 1.61$)---in stark contrast to MOMENT, where the same setting collapses to $0.000$ (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). Moirai lacks an internal RevIN layer, confirming that the collapse is caused by RevIN stripping the temporal statistics the router needs, not by MoE routing failing on temporal representations in general. This sharpens the diagnosis from \S\ref{sec:intro}: the problem is \emph{normalization-induced} co-adaptation, and RR-MoA's raw-signal bypass is the targeted fix.
   436→
   437→\subsection{Top-\texorpdfstring{$k$}{k} Sparse Routing and Task Generalization}
   438→\label{sec:topk}
   439→
   440→Top-2 sparse routing retains $63\%$ of the dense mixture's MSE gain on ETTh1 while activating only $2$ of $5$ experts per sample, bounding active expert FLOPs to $40\%$ of the dense setting (full ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:topk}). The entire RR-MoA stack (${\sim}400$K adapter FLOPs dense, ${\sim}16$K router FLOPs) is ${\sim}0.003\%$ of a single MOMENT-small forward pass, so inference overhead is negligible.
   441→
   442→\textbf{Multi-horizon and task generalization.} RR-MoA wins \textbf{24/24} configurations across horizons $H \in \{96, 192, 336, 720\}$ on ETTh1 and ETTm1 (3 seeds each), with $-38\%$ to $-51\%$ MSE improvement at every horizon (full grid in Appendix~\ref{app:horizon}). The routing advantage is stable from $H{=}96$ to $H{=}720$. RR-MoA also generalizes to imputation (20\% masked reconstruction, 3 seeds): $-44\%$ to $-68\%$ MSE on 3/3 datasets (Appendix~\ref{app:imputation}).
   443→
   444→
   445→\section{Conclusion}
   446→
   447→We identified \emph{normalization-induced} co-adaptation as the cause of MoE routing collapse on TSFMs: RevIN strips the temporal statistics routers need, confirmed by a Moirai control (no RevIN, no collapse). \textbf{RR-MoA} breaks this by routing on the raw pre-normalization signal with a frozen backbone, significantly outperforming all baselines ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) across three backbones (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}), four horizons (Appendix~\ref{app:horizon}), and two tasks. On Moirai, the frozen-backbone paradigm matches DLinear on Weather ($0.209$ vs $0.208$). The \emph{Frozen Paradox}---frozen routing outperforms unfreezing---reverses the standard PEFT heuristic.
   448→
   449→\textbf{Limitations.} (1)~On MOMENT-small, absolute MSE remains higher than supervised baselines; the gap narrows on Moirai but does not vanish on all datasets. (2)~Discrete-tokenized backbones and native MoE TSFMs are not addressed. (3)~The Frozen Paradox analysis is empirical.
```

> AGENT

Now I have a thorough picture of the paper. Here's my honest assessment:

---

## NeurIPS 2026 Readiness Assessment

### Overall: **Borderline Accept / Weak Accept (score ~5.5-6.5/10)**

The paper has improved dramatically from the earlier 5/10 mock review, but there are clear strengths and weaknesses.

---

### Strengths (what works well)

1. **Sharp, falsifiable core finding.** The normalization-induced routing collapse diagnosis is specific, mechanistic, and empirically verified with a clean control (Moirai has no RevIN → no collapse). This is the kind of insight NeurIPS reviewers love — not "our method is better" but "here's *why* the obvious approach fails."

2. **Strong experimental coverage.** 54/54 wins, 3 backbones, 4 horizons, 2 tasks (forecasting + imputation), freeze-level ablations, per-sample routing analysis, independent ensemble control, RevIN ablation. The ablation table design is thorough.

3. **Statistical rigor.** Wilcoxon signed-rank, Bonferroni correction, 3-seed means±std, Cohen's d. This is above average for the venue.

4. **The Frozen Paradox** is genuinely interesting and counter-intuitive — freezing the backbone *helps* routing, reversing the standard NLP PEFT heuristic.

5. **Clean figure design.** The architecture diagram (Fig 1) and routing visualization (Fig 5) tell the story visually.

---

### Weaknesses (what reviewers will attack)

1. **Absolute MSE gap to DLinear is large on MOMENT-small.** ETTh1: 0.690 vs 0.416 (66% worse). The paper acknowledges this honestly and shows Moirai closes the gap on Weather (0.209 vs 0.208), but a reviewer will ask: "Why should I use a frozen TSFM + RR-MoA when a 3-line DLinear beats it by 40-60%?" The deployment motivation paragraph (§1) is good but could be stronger.

2. **AAS feels tacked on.** The paper admits the canonical 5-expert pool outperforms AAS-discovered architectures for routing. AAS's role is reduced to "demonstrating the search space is rich" — but reviewers will ask why it's in the paper at all if the actual RR-MoA experiments don't use it. The narrative coherence ("AAS mines experts → RR-MoA routes them") doesn't hold because the best experts are hand-designed canonical ones.

3. **Limited dataset diversity.** 6 datasets, all from the LTSF benchmark. No non-stationary financial data, no medical/clinical data, no irregular time series. Reviewers increasingly push for diversity beyond ETT/Weather/Electricity.

4. **Single forecast horizon in main results.** H=96 dominates the main tables. The multi-horizon results (H=96-720) are in the appendix. A reviewer might want at least one multi-horizon table in the main text.

5. **No comparison with Moirai-MoE or Time-MoE.** You cite both but don't compare against them. These are native MoE TSFMs — a reviewer will ask how RR-MoA compares to architectures that solve the routing problem differently.

6. **The information-theoretic "argument" is informal.** It's a paragraph of reasoning, not a theorem or bound. Calling it "information-theoretic" sets expectations you don't fully deliver on. Consider calling it a "mechanistic explanation" instead.

7. **T-ZCP is underdeveloped.** The paper itself admits the correlation partly tracks parameter count and needs normalization. Including a half-baked contribution weakens the paper — consider cutting it entirely and focusing on RR-MoA.

---

### Likely Reviewer Scores

| Reviewer archetype | Score | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| TSFM specialist | **6** | Appreciates the routing collapse diagnosis, wants Moirai-MoE comparison |
| MoE/NAS expert | **5-6** | Likes the mechanism, skeptical about AAS relevance, wants formal theory |
| General ML reviewer | **6-7** | Clean paper, good ablations, may not mind the DLinear gap |
| Harsh reviewer | **4-5** | "Frozen backbone loses to DLinear by 40-60%, why not just train from scratch?" |

**Expected average: ~5.5-6.0** — in the "borderline" zone. Could go either way depending on reviewer assignment.

---

### What would push it to Accept (6-7)

1. **Cut T-ZCP entirely** — it dilutes the narrative and invites easy criticism
2. **Cut or heavily demote AAS** — either make it an appendix-only experiment or reframe it as "architecture discovery" that motivated the expert pool design, not a co-equal contribution
3. **Sharpen to a single, clean story:** "RevIN kills MoE routing on TSFMs; raw-signal routing fixes it; freezing the backbone is actually better"
4. **Add a Traffic dataset result** to get 7 datasets
5. **Reframe the DLinear gap** more aggressively: show total FLOPs/deployment cost comparison where frozen-backbone wins
6. **Move multi-horizon table into main text** — 24/24 wins across H=96-720 is impressive

### What would push it to Spotlight (7-8)

- A formal information-theoretic bound (not just intuition) on routing entropy under normalization
- Showing RR-MoA on a decoder backbone (Chronos/TimesFM) in addition to encoder backbones
- Demonstrating the Frozen Paradox on a non-time-series MoE setting (vision/NLP) to show generality

---

**Bottom line:** The core insight (normalization kills routing, raw routing fixes it, freezing paradox) is genuinely novel and well-supported. But the paper tries to do too many things (AAS + RR-MoA + T-ZCP + Frozen Paradox), and the absolute MSE gap to DLinear is the elephant in the room. Streamlining to a focused 3-contribution paper (diagnosis, RR-MoA, Frozen Paradox) would significantly improve chances.

#### 4.1 **CORE RR-MoA Implementation** ✓ COMPLETE

**`run_rr_moa.py` (657 lines)**
- Implements **RawRoutedMoA** class: routes on raw input (not hidden states) to avoid normalization collapse
- **Router design:** Conv1d(1→16, k=32, stride=16) + AdaptiveAvgPool + Linear(64→K)
- **Expert pool:** Selectable between canonical (5 simple heads) or macro (5 AAS-discovered)
- **Sparse routing:** Top-K selection with load-balance loss
- **Training:** 15 epochs, Adam optimizer, frozen backbone
- **Output:** JSON with {dataset, mse, routing_weights, entropy, per-expert_predictions}
- **Usage:**
  ```bash
  python scripts/run_rr_moa.py --dataset ETTh1 --top-k 2 --unfreeze frozen
  python scripts/run_rr_moa.py --dataset Weather --expert-pool macro  # Uses AAS experts
  ```

**`run_adamix.py` (465 lines)**
- Standard MoE baseline that routes on **hidden states** (not raw)
- Demonstrates collapse: entropy → 0.000±0.000 when backbone unfrozen
- Same expert architecture and training loop as RR-MoA for fair comparison

#### 4.2 **Baseline Implementations** ✓ COMPLETE

**`run_dlinear_baseline.py`**
- Simple linear model: `Linear(input_len=512 → output_len=96)` trained from scratch
- No backbone, no adapter — pure supervised baseline on normalized data
- Used to contextualize absolute MSE numbers against a lightweight supervised model
- **Output:** JSON with mse/mae in denormalized units

**`run_trace_baseline.py`**
- TRACE-inspired adapters (Li & Zhu 2025) implemented in PyTorch
- Three variants:
  1. `trace_reconstructed`: Attention pooling + factorized head (d → 64 → H)
  2. `trace_full`: Multi-scale Conv1d (k=3,7) with gated importance weighting
  3. `lora_best`: Best hand-designed LoRA adapter from discrete config space
- Evaluated on test set at 15 epochs
- **Output:** JSON with per-baseline results

**`run_lora_baseline.py`**
- Standard LoRA adapter on MOMENT backbone
- Configurable rank, target modules, layer placement
- Fine-tunes both adapter and head

#### 4.3 **Code Evolution (LLM-Guided Architecture Search)** ✓ COMPLETE

**`run_standard_evolution.py` (394 lines)**
- Main entry point for evolving adapters on a dataset
- **Data loading:** Chronological splits (train/val/test) with StandardScaler
- **Evolution:** GPT-4o generates adapter code → validate → train on val → select top fitness
- **Output:** JSON with evolved code, fitness, MSE at 15 epochs
- **Cross-backbone support:** Detects backbone type (moment/chronos/moirai) and calls appropriate feature extraction
- **Usage:**


**`run_code_evolution.py`** (older entry point, similar functionality)

- Compares code evolution vs discrete search vs random templates

```
Here is my analysis and design for formalizing the theoretical content of the paper. I will propose two theorems, assess each honestly, and recommend a strategy.

## Assessment of the Four Candidate Directions

Before diving into designs, let me be candid about each direction:

**Direction 1 (Mutual information bound):** This is the strongest candidate. The data processing inequality (DPI) gives you I(X; E) >= I(N(X); E) for free whenever N is a deterministic function (RevIN). But stating just the DPI is trivial. The non-trivial part is quantifying the gap and connecting it to routing quality. This can be made rigorous and insightful.

**Direction 2 (Gradient co-adaptation convergence):** This is genuinely hard to prove rigorously. Showing convergence to a single expert under coupled dynamics requires strong assumptions about the loss landscape, and any realistic assumptions would be contestable. The proof would require a simplified model (e.g., linear gate, quadratic loss) that reviewers may dismiss as too restrictive. I recommend against this as a main theorem -- it is better left as a mechanistic narrative supported by Figure 3.

**Direction 3 (Frozen routing optimality):** Very hard to formalize without trivializing. The claim "frozen is better" depends on the specific optimization trajectory, not just information content. Any provable version would need such strong assumptions that it would not be convincing.

**Direction 4 (Variance reduction bound):** This is quantifiable and connects directly to the empirical findings, but alone it feels like a dressed-up calculation. It works best as a corollary of Theorem 1.

## Recommended Strategy: Two Propositions

I recommend **one main theorem** (Proposition 1, in the main text) and **one supporting proposition** (Proposition 2, stated in main text, proof in appendix). Together they tell a complete story: Proposition 1 gives the information-theoretic foundation, Proposition 2 gives the operational consequence for routing.

---

### Proposition 1: Normalization Reduces Routing Mutual Information (with Quantified Gap)

**Statement (precise):**

Let X be a random variable representing input windows drawn from a distribution P over R^L. Define the RevIN operator N(x) = (x - mu(x)) / sigma(x), where mu(x) = (1/L) sum_t x_t and sigma(x) = sqrt((1/L) sum_t (x_t - mu(x))^2). Let E denote any discrete expert assignment variable E in {1, ..., K} that is a deterministic function of the router's input, i.e., E = argmax_k [G_psi(z)]_k for some router G_psi.

Then for any router G_psi:

**I(X; E) >= I(N(X); E)**

with equality if and only if N is a sufficient statistic for E under P -- that is, iff X and E are conditionally independent given N(X).

Moreover, if (mu, sigma, s) are mutually independent under P (where s = N(x)), then:

**I(X; E) - I(N(X); E) >= I(mu, sigma; E | s)**

and this gap is lower-bounded by:

**I(X; E) - I(N(X); E) >= H(E) - H(E | mu, sigma)**

whenever E is conditionally independent of s given (mu, sigma).

**Proof sketch:**
- Part 1: Immediate from the Data Processing Inequality. N is a deterministic function, so the Markov chain X -> N(X) -> E (when routing on normalized input) gives I(X;E) >= I(N(X);E). The equality condition is the standard DPI equality characterization.
- Part 2: Under the independence assumption, I(X;E) = I(mu, sigma, s; E) = I(s; E) + I(mu, sigma; E | s) by the chain rule of MI. Since I(N(X); E) = I(s; E), the gap is exactly I(mu, sigma; E | s).
- Part 3: The final bound follows when routing depends primarily on (mu, sigma): if E is conditionally independent of s given (mu, sigma), then I(mu, sigma; E | s) = I(mu, sigma; E) = H(E) - H(E | mu, sigma). This is maximized when (mu, sigma) fully determine E and H(E) = log K.

**Difficulty of full proof:** Moderate. Part 1 is a textbook application of DPI. Part 2 requires the mutual independence assumption which is non-trivial but defensible for time series (after channel standardization, the shape of a window is approximately independent of its local mean and scale -- this is the whole point of RevIN). Part 3 requires the conditional independence assumption which is an idealization but directly testable from Figure 5 data.

**Reviewer reception:** This is the sweet spot. Part 1 alone would be trivial (just DPI). But Parts 2 and 3 make it non-trivial: they decompose the information loss into a quantity that is (a) directly interpretable in terms of the statistics RevIN strips, and (b) empirically measurable from the routing visualization data. The conditional independence assumption E _||_ s | (mu, sigma) is directly supported by Figure 5, where expert selection clusters cleanly by amplitude/volatility regardless of waveform shape. A theory-minded reviewer will appreciate that the bound is tight in the regime your data occupies, and that the decomposition explains both WHY RevIN hurts (it removes I(mu, sigma; E|s)) and WHEN it would not hurt (when all routing information is in the shape).

**Honest assessment:** The DPI part is a known result. What is genuinely new is the decomposition specific to RevIN's structure: the (mu, sigma, s) factorization is special to instance normalization, and the conclusion that the information gap equals the routing information in the stripped statistics is specific to this paper's setting. This is a legitimate, non-trivial application of information theory to explain a new empirical phenomenon, not a dressed-up tautology.

## Final Recommendation: One Strong Theorem + One Clean Corollary

After careful consideration, I recommend the following approach:

### Theorem 1 (Main Text): Routing Information Decomposition Under Instance Normalization

This is the information-theoretic result from my Proposition 1 above. It should be stated in the main text (5-6 lines) with a brief proof sketch, and the full proof in the appendix.

**Precise statement for the paper:**

> **Theorem 1** (Routing Information Loss Under RevIN). Let X be a random input window and E in {1,...,K} be the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router. Define the RevIN map N: x -> (x - mu(x))/sigma(x) and let S = N(X), M = mu(X), Sigma = sigma(X). Then:
>
> (i) I(X; E) >= I(S; E)  (Data Processing Inequality)
>
> (ii) If (M, Sigma) _||_ S (independence of location-scale from shape), then
>     I(X; E) = I(S; E) + I(M, Sigma; E | S)
>     and the gap I(M, Sigma; E | S) = I(M, Sigma; E) >= 0.
>
> (iii) If additionally E _||_ S | (M, Sigma) (expert assignment depends only on location-scale statistics), then
>     I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E) - H(E | M, Sigma)
>     which equals H(E) (the full routing entropy, maximally log K) when (M, Sigma) determine E.

**Proof:** Part (i): N is deterministic, so X -> N(X) = S forms a Markov chain whenever routing uses S. DPI gives I(X;E) >= I(S;E). Part (ii): Chain rule: I(X;E) = I(M, Sigma, S; E) = I(S;E) + I(M,Sigma; E|S). Under (M,Sigma) _||_ S, the conditional I(M,Sigma; E|S) = I(M,Sigma; E) since knowing S provides no information about (M,Sigma). Part (iii): I(M,Sigma; E) = H(E) - H(E|M,Sigma). When (M,Sigma) determine E, H(E|M,Sigma)=0. QED.

**Difficulty:** The proof itself is straightforward (chain rule + independence). The contribution is the modeling choice: recognizing that RevIN's (mu, sigma, s) decomposition creates a natural information-theoretic decomposition, and that the independence/conditional-independence assumptions are testable from the paper's own data.

**Reviewer reception:** Positive. Part (i) alone would be dismissed as trivial. The full theorem with parts (ii)-(iii) provides a quantitative decomposition that (a) identifies *which* information is lost (the location-scale statistics), (b) gives conditions under which the loss is maximal (when routing depends entirely on what RevIN strips), and (c) is directly validated by Figure 5's routing analysis. A good reviewer will note the assumptions are idealizations, but the paper already provides the empirical validation. This is the kind of "simple but insightful" theorem that NeurIPS spotlights value -- it is not technically hard, but it crystallizes the mechanism.

### Proposition 2 (Main Text, Proof in Appendix): Softmax Entropy Bound from Input Variance Reduction

**Precise statement:**

> **Proposition 2** (Logit Variance Controls Routing Entropy). Let g = Wz + b in R^K be linear gate logits for router input z, with routing distribution p_k = softmax(g)_k. Let Sigma_z = Cov(z) and define the total logit variance V = sum_k Var[g_k] = tr(W Sigma_z W^T). Then the expected routing entropy satisfies:
>
> E_z[H(softmax(Wz+b))] >= log K - V / (2 ln 2)
>
> Consequently, for a router with fixed weights W applied to raw input (z = x, Sigma_z = Sigma_x) vs. RevIN input (z = s, Sigma_z = Sigma_s):
>
> E[H(softmax(Ws+b))] >= E[H(softmax(Wx+b))]
>
> whenever Sigma_x - Sigma_s is positive semidefinite (i.e., normalization reduces input variance in all directions). The routing entropy floor under RevIN is closer to log K (uniform, non-discriminative routing).

**Proof sketch:** The first inequality uses the Gibbs inequality: H(softmax(g)) >= log K - D_KL(softmax(g) || uniform) >= log K - (1/(2ln2)) * sum_k (p_k - 1/K)^2 * K. The quadratic term is bounded by the logit variance via the sensitivity of softmax. Specifically, for any g, ||softmax(g) - 1/K||^2 <= ||g - mean(g)||^2 / 4 (softmax is 1-Lipschitz in the L2 -> L2 sense on the centered logits). The conclusion about RevIN follows because Sigma_s is dominated by Sigma_x (normalization cannot increase variance), so tr(W Sigma_s W^T) <= tr(W Sigma_x W^T).

**Difficulty:** Moderate. The softmax Lipschitz bound is well-known. The key technical step is connecting logit variance to routing entropy, which requires care with the constants. The PSD ordering Sigma_x >= Sigma_s needs verification: this holds because x = mu*1 + sigma*s, so Cov(x) includes additional rank-1 and cross terms that are PSD.

**Reviewer reception:** This is the operational consequence of Theorem 1, translated into the routing entropy language used throughout the paper. It directly explains *why* RevIN-routed entropy stays high (near log K = 1.609) yet non-discriminative. A reviewer can check: the RevIN router has entropy 1.50-1.57 (Table 4, the RevIN router ablation), very close to max 1.609, consistent with the lower bound being tight. This is a clean, useful result that connects to the numbers in the paper.

**Honest assessment of non-triviality:** Proposition 2 is closer to a "dressed-up calculation" than Theorem 1. The softmax Lipschitz bound is standard, and the variance ordering under normalization is straightforward. However, the combination -- connecting instance normalization to routing entropy via logit variance -- is new to this setting and directly explains the paper's central empirical phenomenon. For a systems/empirical paper aiming at spotlight, this level of formalization is appropriate. A pure-theory paper would need more, but this is an applied contribution.
```

```
### 2A. Formal Proposition: RevIN Collapses Routing Mutual Information

The paper already has the informal argument at lines 362-363. Formalize it as a proposition.

**Proposition 2 (Routing Signal Collapse under Instance Normalization)**:
Let x_i be a time series window decomposed as x_i = mu_i + sigma_i * s_i where mu_i is the mean, sigma_i the standard deviation, and s_i the shape. Let G_psi be a routing network producing logits g_i = G_psi(x_i). Define the routing signal strength as Var_i[g_i]. Under RevIN, x_i -> s_i = (x_i - mu_i)/sigma_i, eliminating two of three variance components. Formally:

Var_i[G_psi(x_i^RevIN)] <= Var_i[G_psi(x_i)] - Var_i[G_psi(mu_i, sigma_i | s_i)]

where the second term is the conditional variance explained by the removed statistics. When mu_i and sigma_i are the primary discriminative features (as in non-stationary time series), this bound shows RevIN removes the dominant signal, approaching uniform routing.

**Proof sketch**: Decompose the total variance via the law of total variance. RevIN sets mu_i = 0, sigma_i = 1 for all i, collapsing the between-group variance to zero.

This is not a deep theorem, but it is:
1. Non-trivial (requires formal setup)
2. Testable (the paper already validates it empirically)
3. Explanatory (connects to all three empirical observations)

**Additional theory option**: A proposition about the gradient co-adaptation feedback loop. Under linear approximation of the router and a single-step gradient update, show that the entropy of routing weights is monotonically decreasing when backbone gradients flow through the routing path, establishing the collapse as a fixed-point attractor.

**Files**: `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/main.tex` -- insert after line 362 (information-theoretic argument paragraph), with full proof in appendix after line 1021
**Effort**: 6-8 hours (formulation + proof + writing)
**Impact**: HIGH -- transforms "informal argument" into a checkable theoretical result; fills the theory checklist item

## 7. RISK ASSESSMENT

**Things that could go wrong**:

1. **Traffic experiments fail**: The data file exists but the pipeline may need adjustments for 862 channels. Test with a single seed first before launching the full grid. If it fails, the paper still works with 6 datasets -- just address the omission in limitations.

2. **Proposition 2 is too simple for reviewers**: The variance decomposition is elementary. Mitigate by pairing it with empirical validation (Table 4 already does this) and by acknowledging in the text: "While this result follows from standard variance decomposition, it precisely predicts all three empirical observations and was not previously identified in the TSFM literature."

3. **Page limit**: NeurIPS 2026 allows 9 pages main text. Current main text runs to line 451 (roughly 8-9 pages depending on float placement). After removing AAS material and adding theory + related work, this should remain within budget. Monitor carefully.

4. **AAS reviewers**: Some reviewers may have been assigned specifically for the AAS angle. By keeping AAS in the appendix with full details, you preserve it for those reviewers while not letting it dilute the main story.
```

```
  1397→\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
  1398→\label{app:deployment}
  1399→
  1400→The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
  1401→
  1402→\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Retraining a separate DLinear per tenant does not amortize the backbone cost and forfeits zero-shot transfer.
  1403→
  1404→\textbf{(ii) On-device and edge deployment.} One backbone is shipped with the device image; per-site adapters are updated over low-bandwidth links. Collecting each site's training data centrally is often impossible for privacy or latency reasons.
  1405→
  1406→\textbf{(iii) Cross-task reuse.} The same frozen backbone drives forecasting, imputation, and classification via different expert pools. We demonstrate the first two tasks explicitly in the main text.
  1407→
  1408→\end{document}
```

- Strong correlation (r ≥ 0.8) = theory predicts which datasets benefit most

- With n=6 datasets, even r=0.9 has limited power but shows predictive ability

## FEASIBILITY REPORT: Disabling RevIN in MOMENT for Ablation Study

Disabling RevIN inside the MOMENT model is **entirely practical and straightforward**. No architectural barriers exist.

#### **Change 1: `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/model.py`** (~10 lines)

Modify `load_moment()` function:

```python
def load_moment(device: str = "cpu", model_name: str = "AutonLab/MOMENT-1-small", disable_revin: bool = False) -> nn.Module:
    """Load MOMENT pretrained model (small, base, or large)."""
    from momentfm import MOMENTPipeline

    model = MOMENTPipeline.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        model_kwargs={"task_name": "reconstruction"},
    )
    model.init()
    model = model.to(device)
    model.eval()
    
    # NEW: Optionally disable RevIN normalization
    if disable_revin:
        class IdentityNormalizer(nn.Module):
            def forward(self, x, mode="norm", mask=None):
                return x  # Pass through unchanged
        model.normalizer = IdentityNormalizer()
    
    return model
```

Then propagate the parameter through:

- `load_backbone()` (~2 lines) - add `disable_revin` parameter
- `build_adapted_model()` (~2 lines) - add `disable_revin` parameter

  3. `embed()`: Input normalization (norm) only
- These are all in the MOMENT pipeline, **not in your code**

#### ✓ **Why replacement is safe:**
- RevIN's interface is simple: `forward(x, mode="norm"/"denorm", mask=None)` → returns tensor

```
     1→"""Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA).
     2→
     3→Fixes the AdaMix/MoE failure: standard routers collapse because the TSFM
     4→normalization cascade (RevIN + LayerNorm) destroys hidden-state heterogeneity.
     5→RR-MoA routes on the RAW input instead, preserving the spectral and
     6→statistical diversity needed for per-sample adapter selection.
     7→
     8→Key insight: the backbone processes deep semantics, while a lightweight
     9→router reads the raw signal to select the adapter topology per-sample.
    10→
    11→Usage:
    12→    python scripts/run_rr_moa.py --dataset ETTh1
    13→    python scripts/run_rr_moa.py --dataset ETTh1 --top-k 2 --unfreeze frozen
    14→"""
    15→
    16→import argparse
    17→import json
    18→import os
```

```
     1→"""Dataset download and preprocessing for feasibility experiment."""
     2→
     3→import io
     4→import numpy as np
     5→import pandas as pd
     6→import torch
     7→import torch.nn.functional as F
     8→from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
     9→from urllib.request import urlopen
    10→
    11→
    12→ETT_BASE_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small"
    13→WEATHER_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thuml/Time-Series-Library/main/dataset/weather/weather.csv"
    14→MOMENT_SEQ_LEN = 512
    15→
    16→
    17→def extract_trend(X: torch.Tensor, kernel_size: int = 25) -> torch.Tensor:
    18→    """Extract trend via 1D average pooling (paper Eq. 1).
    19→
    20→    Args:
    21→        X: (batch, seq_len) tensor
    22→        kernel_size: smoothing window size
    23→
    24→    Returns:
    25→        Trend tensor of same shape as X
    26→    """
    27→    if X.dim() == 2:
    28→        X = X.unsqueeze(1)  # (batch, 1, seq_len)
    29→    pad = kernel_size // 2
    30→    X_padded = F.pad(X, (pad, pad), mode="reflect")
    31→    trend = F.avg_pool1d(X_padded, kernel_size, stride=1)
    32→    return trend.squeeze(1)
    33→
    34→
    35→def _load_csv_forecasting(url: str, name: str, seq_len: int = MOMENT_SEQ_LEN,
    36→                          stride: int = 64, max_samples: int = None) -> dict:
    37→    """Generic loader for CSV forecasting datasets (ETT, Weather, etc.).
    38→
    39→    Expects CSV with a date column followed by numeric feature columns.
    40→    Returns dict with 'samples' (n, seq_len) numpy array and 'name'.
    41→    """
    42→    response = urlopen(url)
    43→    df = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(response.read()))
    44→    # Drop date column, keep numeric columns
    45→    values = df.iloc[:, 1:].values.astype(np.float32)
    46→
    47→    n_timesteps, n_channels = values.shape
    48→    windows = []
    49→    for start in range(0, n_timesteps - seq_len + 1, stride):
    50→        window = values[start : start + seq_len]
    51→        windows.append(window)
    52→    windows = np.stack(windows)
    53→
    54→    n_windows = windows.shape[0]
    55→    samples = windows.transpose(0, 2, 1).reshape(n_windows * n_channels, seq_len)
    56→
    57→    if max_samples and len(samples) > max_samples:
    58→        rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    59→        idx = rng.choice(len(samples), max_samples, replace=False)
    60→        samples = samples[idx]
```

```
    53→def load_standard_data(dataset_name, forecast_horizon=96, max_samples=5000):
    54→    """Load with standard chronological splits.
    55→
    56→    Returns ``(splits, n_ch)`` where ``splits`` is a dict keyed by ``"train"``,
    57→    ``"val"``, ``"test"`` whose values are ``(X, Y)`` numpy arrays. For
    58→    backwards compatibility the core two-tuple entry is unchanged, but the
    59→    dict also carries extra metadata used by denormalized-MSE reporting:
    60→
    61→    - ``splits["_scaler"]`` : the fitted sklearn ``StandardScaler``
    62→    - ``splits["<name>_ch"]`` : per-sample channel index array aligned with
    63→      ``splits["<name>"]``. Since DataLoader iterates the test tensor with
    64→      ``shuffle=False``, this can be used to denormalize predictions back to
    65→      original units via
    66→      ``pred * scaler.scale_[ch] + scaler.mean_[ch]``.
    67→    """
    68→    if dataset_name.startswith("ETT"):
    69→        url = "%s/%s.csv" % (ETT_BASE, dataset_name)
    70→        df = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(urlopen(url).read()))
    71→    elif dataset_name == "Weather":
    72→        local_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "data", "weather.csv")
    73→        df = pd.read_csv(local_path)
    74→    elif dataset_name == "Electricity":
    75→        local_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "data", "electricity.csv")
    76→        df = pd.read_csv(local_path)
    77→    else:
    78→        raise ValueError("Unknown dataset: %s" % dataset_name)
    79→
    80→    values = df.iloc[:, 1:].values.astype(np.float32)
    81→    n_ch = values.shape[1]
    82→
    83→    if dataset_name in SPLITS:
    84→        n_train, n_val, n_test = SPLITS[dataset_name]
    85→    else:
    86→        # Default 60/20/20
    87→        n_total = len(values)
    88→        n_train = int(0.6 * n_total)
    89→        n_val = int(0.2 * n_total)
    90→        n_test = n_total - n_train - n_val
    91→    scaler = StandardScaler()
    92→    scaler.fit(values[:n_train])
    93→
    94→    splits = {"_scaler": scaler}
    95→    for name, start, length in [
    96→        ("train", 0, n_train),
    97→        ("val", n_train, n_val),
    98→        ("test", n_train + n_val, n_test),
    99→    ]:
   100→        data = scaler.transform(values[start:start+length]).astype(np.float32)
   101→        total_len = INPUT_LEN + forecast_horizon
   102→        X, Y, CH = [], [], []
   103→        for ch in range(n_ch):
   104→            s = data[:, ch]
   105→            for i in range(0, len(s) - total_len + 1):
   106→                X.append(s[i:i+INPUT_LEN])
   107→                Y.append(s[i+INPUT_LEN:i+total_len])
```

```json
{
  "file_path": "/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/analyze_routing_signal_ratio.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Compute per-dataset routing signal ratio R and correlate with RR-MoA improvement.\n\nValidates Theorem 1's prediction: datasets where RevIN strips more information\n(higher R = Var(mu,sigma) / Var(shape)) should show larger RR-MoA improvements.\n\nUsage:\n    python scripts/analyze_routing_signal_ratio.py\n\"\"\"\n\nimport io\nimport json\nimport os\nimport sys\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom urllib.request import urlopen\n\nsys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))\n\nETT_BASE = \"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small\"\nINPUT_LEN = 512\nSTRIDE = 64\n\n\ndef load_raw_windows(dataset_name):\n    \"\"\"Load raw (pre-StandardScaler) windows for a dataset.\n\n    Returns array of shape (n_windows, seq_len) — one window per channel-sample.\n    \"\"\"\n    data_dir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), \"..\", \"data\")\n\n    if dataset_name.startswith(\"ETT\"):\n        url = \"%s/%s.csv\" % (ETT_BASE, dataset_name)\n        df = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(urlopen(url).read()))\n    elif dataset_name == \"Weather\":\n        df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(data_dir, \"weather.csv\"))\n    elif dataset_name == \"Electricity\":\n        df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(data_dir, \"electricity.csv\"))\n    elif dataset_name == \"Traffic\":\n        df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(data_dir, \"traffic.csv\"))\n    else:\n        raise ValueError(\"Unknown dataset: %s\" % dataset_name)\n\n    values = df.iloc[:, 1:].values.astype(np.float32)\n    n_ch = values.shape[1]\n\n    # Create sliding windows (raw, no scaler) for each channel\n    windows = []\n    for ch in range(n_ch):\n        s = values[:, ch]\n        for i in range(0, len(s) - INPUT_LEN + 1, STRIDE):\n            windows.append(s[i:i + INPUT_LEN])\n\n    windows = np.stack(windows)  # (n_windows, INPUT_LEN)\n\n    # Subsample if too large\n    if len(windows) > 10000:\n        rng = np.random.default_rng(42)\n        idx = rng.choice(len(windows), 10000, replace=False)\n        windows = windows[idx]\n\n    return windows\n\n\ndef compute_routing_signal_ratio(windows):\n    \"\"\"Compute R = Var(mu, sigma) / Var(shape) for a set of raw windows.\n\n    mu_w = per-window mean (what RevIN strips)\n    sigma_w = per-window std (what RevIN strips)\n    s_w = (x_w - mu_w) / sigma_w = shape (what RevIN preserves)\n    \"\"\"\n    # Per-window location-scale statistics\n    mu_w = windows.mean(axis=1)       # (n_windows,)\n    sigma_w = windows.std(axis=1)     # (n_windows,)\n\n    # Shape after RevIN\n    sigma_safe = np.clip(sigma_w, 1e-8, None)\n    shape_w = (windows - mu_w[:, None]) / sigma_safe[:, None]\n\n    # Variance of location-scale statistics\n    var_mu = np.var(mu_w)\n    var_sigma = np.var(sigma_w)\n    location_scale_var = var_mu + var_sigma\n\n    # Variance of shape (average variance across temporal positions)\n    shape_var = np.mean(np.var(shape_w, axis=0))\n\n    ratio = location_scale_var / max(shape_var, 1e-8)\n\n    return {\n        \"var_mu\": float(var_mu),\n        \"var_sigma\": float(var_sigma),\n        \"location_scale_var\": float(location_scale_var),\n        \"shape_var\": float(shape_var),\n        \"ratio_R\": float(ratio),\n    }\n\n\ndef load_rrmoa_improvement(dataset_name):\n    \"\"\"Load RR-MoA improvement (Δ%) from result JSONs, averaged over 3 seeds.\"\"\"\n    results_dir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), \"..\", \"results\", \"rr_moa\")\n    deltas = []\n    for seed in [42, 43, 44]:\n        path = os.path.join(results_dir, \"%s_H96_K5_top2_frozen_%d.json\" % (dataset_name, seed))\n        if not os.path.exists(path):\n            continue\n        with open(path) as f:\n            d = json.load(f)\n        rrmoa_mse = d[\"rr_moa\"][\"mse\"]\n        # Get best baseline MSE\n        if d.get(\"baselines\"):\n            best_bl = min(d[\"baselines\"].values(), key=lambda x: x[\"mse\"])[\"mse\"]\n            delta = (rrmoa_mse - best_bl) / best_bl * 100\n            deltas.append(delta)\n\n    if not deltas:\n        return None\n    return float(np.mean(deltas))\n\n\ndef main():\n    datasets = [\"ETTh1\", \"ETTh2\", \"ETTm1\", \"ETTm2\", \"Weather\", \"Electricity\"]\n\n    print(\"=\" * 80)\n    print(\"ROUTING SIGNAL RATIO ANALYSIS (Theorem 1 Prediction)\")\n    print(\"=\" * 80)\n    print()\n\n    results = []\n    for ds in datasets:\n        print(\"Processing %s...\" % ds)\n        try:\n            windows = load_raw_windows(ds)\n            stats = compute_routing_signal_ratio(windows)\n            delta = load_rrmoa_improvement(ds)\n            stats[\"dataset\"] = ds\n            stats[\"delta_pct\"] = delta\n            stats[\"n_windows\"] = len(windows)\n            results.append(stats)\n            print(\"  R = %.4f  (Var_mu=%.4f, Var_sigma=%.4f, Var_shape=%.4f)  Δ%% = %s\" % (\n                stats[\"ratio_R\"], stats[\"var_mu\"], stats[\"var_sigma\"],\n                stats[\"shape_var\"],\n                \"%.1f%%\" % delta if delta is not None else \"N/A\"))\n        except Exception as e:\n            print(\"  ERROR: %s\" % e)\n\n    print()\n\n    # Correlation analysis\n    valid = [(r[\"ratio_R\"], r[\"delta_pct\"]) for r in results if r[\"delta_pct\"] is not None]\n    if len(valid) >= 4:\n        from scipy.stats import spearmanr, pearsonr\n        Rs = [v[0] for v in valid]\n        Ds = [v[1] for v in valid]  # Note: Δ is negative (improvement), more negative = better\n        # We expect: higher R → more negative Δ (larger improvement)\n        rho_s, p_s = spearmanr(Rs, Ds)\n        rho_p, p_p = pearsonr(Rs, Ds)\n        print(\"CORRELATION (R vs Δ%%, n=%d):\" % len(valid))\n        print(\"  Spearman ρ = %.3f  (p = %.4f)\" % (rho_s, p_s))\n        print(\"  Pearson  r = %.3f  (p = %.4f)\" % (rho_p, p_p))\n        print()\n        print(\"  Interpretation: negative correlation means higher R → larger improvement\")\n        print(\"  (more negative Δ%%), validating Theorem 1.\")\n    else:\n        print(\"Not enough data points for correlation (need ≥ 4, have %d)\" % len(valid))\n\n    # Save results\n    out_path = \"results/analysis/routing_signal_ratio.json\"\n    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_path), exist_ok=True)\n    with open(out_path, \"w\") as f:\n        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)\n    print(\"\\nSaved to %s\" % out_path)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n"
}
```
